chapter_theme: Akananuru 261 to 280, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: paalai roads seen from both ends of an elopement (the man recalling her shyness, two mothers at the empty house), wives counting seasons and refusing to blame the absent man, hill courtships threatened by a mother's Murugu worship and a midnight storm, neythal suitors who would marry by servitude, and marutham quarrels in which the wife or the courtesan speaks. Puram matter (Minili's vow, Evvi's victory feast, the Nandas' hoard, hero-stones, Kuttuvan's Kazhumalam) supplies the measures for private feeling.

261.reading: Back home, the man tells the friend how on the elopement road the girl, flowers of the forest pressed into her hair and bangles chiming, was too shy to walk ahead when he asked to see her back, and stood with bowed head, so he slowed and they camped in the wild, hearing a tiger roar over a killed elephant and the drums of drunk bowmen in their fort.
261.nuance: The danger of the road (tiger, bowmen's drums) comes only after the moment of shyness and is told as background to it: the memory he brings back to the friend is her நாண் on the road, not the peril. His small joke, asking to see her back, turns flight into courtship.

colophon.thurai: புணர்ந்துடன் போயினகாலை இடைச்சுரத்துப் பட்டதனை மீண்டு வந்த காலத்துத் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers going together through the waste land

comparisons.tenor: her glance, which outdoes a deer's

occasion.words: மீண்டு வந்த காலத்துத் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது

262.reading: Leaving the night meeting, the man tells his heart he is full of joy because her sweet voice came to him smelling of Pekan's rain-wrapped hill, joy like that of Anni Minili, who after the Kosar blinded her father over a cow that strayed into the gram field fasted and wore no clean cloth until Thithiyan killed them, and then let her anger go.
262.nuance: The simile is a whole revenge story: his joy is measured not by a happy thing but by the release of a vow kept through long self-denial, which hints at how long he has waited and suffered. Pekan, the patron known for giving, lends his hill's rain-smell to her speech.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிக்கண் தலைமகளைப் புணர்ந்து நீங்குந் தலைமகன் தன் னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the joy of a secret meeting on the hill

comparisons.tenor: his joy, like Minili's when her vow of anger was fulfilled

263.reading: A mother whose daughter has gone off with a bold young man across the sun-scorched waste, where bowmen watch from raised ground for travellers, says that had she known the girl's resolve she would gladly have married her to him in her rich house, splendid as Kothai's spear-guarded Vanji.
263.nuance: The lament is not against the elopement but against having been left out of it: the mother would have given the wedding herself. The closing lines, about the untroubled sleep on the young breast, are hard to construe; they may picture the girl asleep in his arms as she would have been at home.

colophon.thurai: மகட் போக்கிய தாய் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl taken across the waste by her lover

comparisons.tenor: her own rich house, like Kothai's capital Vanji

264.reading: As the cold season sets in, with musundai flowers white as stars, cowherds coming home in the rain with their wet garlands and the water running down every street, the woman asks whether the men in the fierce king's camp, ringed by elephants at night, even if they do not know her plight, at least know their own.
264.nuance: The cowherds going home at the rain's appointed time are the silent contrast: everyone returns with the season except the men in the camp. Her barb (they may not know our state, but do they know theirs?) turns pity into reproach.

colophon.thurai: பருவங் கண்டு வன்புறை யெதிரழிந்து தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது; தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains and the cowherds' evening return mark the waiting

comparisons.tenor: the white musundai blossoms, like stars in a cloudless sky

occasion.words: பருவங் கண்டு வன்புறை யெதிரழிந்து தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது

265.reading: Her bangles slipping and her eyes wet, the woman asks her friend what the wealth can be that her man rated above her, crossing the Venkatam wastes where bowmen roast flesh and drink beer: is it as great as the red Himalayan peak, or the treasure the Nandas hid under the Ganges at Pataliputra?
265.nuance: The two guesses are the largest measures of value a Tamil poet could name, one natural and one royal and northern; set against them, her own worth is the unspoken third term. The bowmen eating 'like demons' make the road the price of that wealth.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் ஆற்றாமை மீதூரத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has crossed the waste for wealth, leaving her

comparisons.tenor: the red Himalayan peak, like a creeping flame
the wealth he went for, matched against the Himalaya

comparisons.vehicle: நந்தர் சீர்மிகு பாடலிக் குழீஇக் கங்கை நீர்முதற் கரந்த நிதியம்
comparisons.tenor: the wealth he went for, guessed to be the Nandas' hidden hoard
her hair, rippled like fine sand in shaded water
the bowmen eating fresh meat

occasion.words: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் ஆற்றாமை மீதூரத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது

266.reading: The wife tells her husband that his bathing yesterday in the evening flood with young women, clinging to a float and losing all shame as he gazed at one woman's eyes, is now gossip as loud as the feast at Uraththur after Evvi's men won; that does not grieve her now, but the oath he swore to her by Murugan of Alaivay does.
266.nuance: The point is in the last turn: public scandal she can bear, a broken oath sworn before the god she cannot. The image of peacocks scared by ploughmen's shouts flying in to the temple precinct carries the oath's setting from field to shrine. Lines 10 to 13, Evvi's victory at Uraththur, are syntactically hard; the sense of the simile, a famous loud feast, is clear.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்துவந்து கூடிய தலைமகற்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife confronts a husband back from other women

comparisons.tenor: the gossip about him, as loud as the victory feast at Uraththur

267.reading: When her friend grieves that the man who swore unbreakable oaths has changed for the sake of work, the wife answers that the men who crossed the summer hills, where bears raid iruppai blossoms and monkeys leaping on bamboo scatter its rice to pop on hot rock, are not to blame; her own shoulders are, for letting the bangles slip and not knowing how to hold him.
267.nuance: She shifts blame from the absent man to her own body, a loyal defence that is also an accusation of the friend who called him faithless. The hill scene is crowded with creatures taking and scattering food, abundance in a dry season.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளது ஆற்றாமை கண்டு ஆற்றாளாகிய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone across the waste for his work

comparisons.tenor: the closed iruppai buds, like a wild cat's paw
the white iruppai flowers, like turned ivory
the monkeys' dark faces, as if smeared with ink
the bamboo rice popping on the hot rock, like the crack of a nail

268.reading: The friend, having taken up the man's suit, tells the girl that if she truly loves the lord of the hill where vengai and wild jasmine sweeten a field bloodied by an elephant and tiger, she should say so; for she herself, without consulting the girl dear as life, has already slipped past their father's strict guard and taken on a great blame that is not deserved.
268.nuance: The friend's confession puts the girl in her debt: she has risked the shame already, so the girl can only say yes. The hill whose flower-scent drives off the blood-smell may hint that love will cover the scandal; that reading is traditional and not forced by the poem.

colophon.thurai: குறைவேண்டிப் பின்னின்ற தலைமகனுக்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country and its flowers frame the courtship

comparisons.tenor: the girl, dear to the friend as her own life
their father among his kin, like bamboo with its shoots

269.reading: The friend tells the wife to let her bangles climb back and her hair be dressed, for the man who crossed the road of hero-stones, set where warriors who held off the Mazhavar's spears fell and now washed, smeared with turmeric and crowned with red karanthai, has hurried home at the end of Thai's cool rains to wipe her tears, eyes like the red water-lilies of Vaanan's Sirukudi.
269.nuance: The hero-stones carry no hidden sense of the lovers (the brief's model of a failed iraicchi); they mark the road's danger and its honour. The return is timed by a seaside festival, women bringing sand dolls to the ghat and dancing the kuravai to horn and drum, so comfort arrives with a feast.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man who crossed the waste is reported on his way back

comparisons.tenor: the low hillock, like a she-elephant lying down
the unplanted tall stone that looks as if set up
her eyes, red from weeping, like the red water-lily

270.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where fishermen wear backwater lilies and njazhal, that the girl's shoulders have thinned and her beauty, once like Kuttuvan's Kazhumalam, is wasting as she gazes sleepless at the bay, while he, even on nights when the little black hen-bird in the thorny nest of the sacred tree suffers apart from her mate, thinks only of his own town.
270.nuance: The demand for marriage is made without the word: the friend sets the girl's nights beside his, and lets the unpaired hen-bird make the case. நோகோ யானே, 'shall I grieve, then?', closes on the friend's own helplessness.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறிக்கண் வந்துநீங்குந் தலைமகனைத் தோழி வரைவுகடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, punnai and the shore

comparisons.tenor: the girl's former beauty, like Kuttuvan's rich town Kazhumalam

iraicchi.act: the little hen-bird, not joined with her mate in the nest, suffers through the night
iraicchi.sense: the girl spends the same nights apart from him, so he should marry and not leave her mateless

271.reading: Knowing the girl's mind, the friend tells the man who has announced his journey that if he means to cross the waste where doves peck grit with their mates and the nelli's tart fruit holds back the departing lives of thirsty travellers, may his work prosper; but if the bangles slip from her shoulders, smooth as the bamboo of Aviyan's cloud-capped hill, is there a medicine for her in the land where he will stay?
271.nuance: The road has a remedy for travellers (the nelli that restores them) and the dove that travels with its mate; she will have neither. The blessing on his work is ironic, the real sentence is the closing question.

colophon.thurai: 1செலவுணர்த்திய தோழி தலைமகளது குறிப்பறிந்து தலைமகனைச் செலவழுங்கச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is set on crossing the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: her long soft shoulders, like the joints of bamboo

iraicchi.act: the dove cock goes to the far land together with his small hen and feeds there with her
iraicchi.sense: even the dove takes its mate along on a far journey, while he means to go alone and leave her

272.reading: With the man listening outside, the friend tells the girl how he comes alone through the dark cleft of the hill, his spear lighting the path, wearing a garland of koothalam and wild jasmine whose scent the wind carries into their hut, and how the mother, seeing him so, took him for Murugu, greeted him and scattered red millet in worship of Nedu Vel; what will become of their bond with the lord of the hill?
272.nuance: The friend's comedy has a point: the mother's piety is the measure of how near discovery is, and the man who hears it is told that night visits cannot go on. Who is மெய்ம்மலி உவகையன் and what the mother actually sees are not certain; the reading here takes the comer as the man, mistaken for the god he resembles by spear and garland.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill's cleft, kino, peacock and Murugu

comparisons.tenor: the vengai in flower, gold-like

273.reading: As the new cold season comes, with white herons wheeling like a garland flung across the sky, the woman, wasting with pallor, asks whether he does not know her pain or, knowing it, lacks a heart soft as hers; and she pictures her love-sickness as a great shameless tree, sprouting between her breasts, swelling with the north wind, branching with the town's gossip and budding with scandal over the whole earth, while he does not come.
273.nuance: The tree is built part by part: sprout, trunk, branches of அம்பல், shoots of love, buds of அலர். 'Praised by poets' and 'shameless' make it a public thing, the opposite of a secret love. The poem is about waiting through a season, which is why the inferred thinai is mullai against the colophon's paalai.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவின்கண் தலைமகள் அறிவுமயங்கிச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits through the season he should have returned by

comparisons.tenor: the white herons wheeling in the sky, like a flung koothalam garland
her love-sickness, grown into a great tree fed by gossip

274.reading: Returning, the man tells his charioteer that her town lies in the cool fragrant scrub where, on a midnight of the rainy season, a lone herdsman stands on one leg propped on his staff with his pot, sling and hide, a small fire lit with a drill, the drizzle wetting one side, and his whistle sends the jackal watching his leaping lambs scurrying into the thorn bushes.
274.nuance: The poem is almost all scene; the woman appears only in the last two lines, as one whose chastity is worthy of the mullai flower. The herdsman keeping lone watch over his flock through the rainy night can be felt as a picture of her guarded steadfastness, but he does nothing of the lovers' situation, so it stays scene.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: herdsman, scrubland and mullai at the rainy midnight

275.reading: The mother whose daughter left yesterday with a stranger, trusting his love, across the hot hills where bear cubs and their clan raid the iruppai's white flowers, remembers the girl watering the vayalai on the pandal and playing ball, answering scolding with lisping sweet words, and asks those who have eyes to look at the sand house her small red fingers traced under the nochi.
275.nuance: The last image is the whole grief: a child's sand house still standing after the child has gone into the waste. Lines 4 and 5 (the address வளமனைக் கிழத்தி and the scolding பிதிர்வை நீரை வெண்நீறு ஆக) are obscure, so who is addressed and what she was scolded for cannot be fixed. The bear cubs feeding with their kin are scene, though a reader may feel the contrast with the girl who left hers.

colophon.thurai: மகட் போக்கிய 1தாய் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl gone through the waste with her lover

276.reading: The courtesan, so that the wife's women will hear, says that the lord of the ford, who slips aside like a thief creeping into a guarded house, as the stork stalks the white vaalai fish softly so its steps are not known, may come to her street; before his wives' eyes she will seize his garland and cloth and bind him with her hair like the bull elephant the Aryans lure with a she-elephant, or else let her mother-guarded beauty go to waste like the wealth of a man who hoarded and gave nothing to those who asked.
276.nuance: Her oath ends on the image of the miser's wealth: beauty not spent is wasted as wealth not given is wasted. She speaks as a challenger, and the furtive stork makes the husband a thief before the wives.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகட்ருப் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பப் பரத்தை சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: pond, fish and stork of the town by the fields

comparisons.tenor: the stork stalking the fish, and through it the man slipping off to her
the man she will bind with her hair
her beauty left to waste unless she wins him

ullurai.tenor: the husband stealing away to the courtesan while hiding it from his wives

pairs.situation: he goes softly, afraid his wives will learn where he went
he goes to take his pleasure with the courtesan
he slips aside from the household's ford to her street

ullurai.speaker_fit: the courtesan speaks freely as one outside the household (porul 7.29), with the stork and fish of the marutham pond

277.reading: Her forehead's glow fading like the moon by day, the woman tells her friend that before the man returns from the dry road, where a tiger that cannot bear its hungry mate's hunger watches for a bristly boar and travellers rest in the spotted shade of hollow trees, the spring has come, the murukku in flame-red bloom like the fighting cock's neck, its blossoms shaken down by bees; he has not come.
277.nuance: The season is announced with violent colour, a domestic cock's fighting hackles for the red flowers. The tiger hunting for its mate makes the road itself an argument for why he went and why he should return.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குப் பருவங்கண் டழிந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the dry road and the coming of spring

comparisons.vehicle: தண்கதிர் மண்டிலம் அவிர்அறச் சாஅய்ப் பகலழி தோற்றம் போலப்
comparisons.tenor: her forehead losing its glow, like the moon by day
the boar's coarse bristles, like palmyra fibres
the cock's dense hackles, like leaping flame
the murukku blossoms, like the fighting cock's fiery neck

iraicchi.act: the tiger, unable to bear his mate's hunger, lies in wait to hunt for her
iraicchi.sense: a male who goes out for his mate's need, as he did, should bring what he hunts home to her, yet the season has come and he has not

278.reading: With the man listening outside, the friend tells the girl that the clouds drawn from the eastern sea have massed over the mountain at midnight like the shields of kings' armies, with lightning and thunder; tomorrow the falls will come down bending the bamboo to the ford of their town, and they will bathe in that water, which played on the mountain of the man who wasted her beauty, to ease the pain of their sleepless nights.
278.nuance: The storm warns the listening man that the night path is dangerous and the waiting long; the bath in water from his own mountain is the only contact with him left to them, which presses him toward marriage without naming it.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிக்கண் தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain at midnight

comparisons.tenor: the massed dark clouds, like rows of shields in kings' armies
the lightning, like a banner raised on its pole
her body, dark as a sapphire

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறிக்கண் தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

279.reading: Setting out for wealth, the man tells his heart that the fire of the old saying, that only men who never leave their wives' breasts can bear to live in one town watching friends in want and kin in distress, burned in him night and day and was not quenched by the rain of effort; but while he toils in the waste, how will she fare in the mornings when the koel wakes sleeping pairs, walking softly like a swan, helpless of heart?
279.nuance: Duty to friends and kin is the reason given for leaving, not desire for wealth itself, and it is put as a proverb he cannot answer. The swan's gait and the paired sleepers waked by the koel make her mornings the cost. Lines 11 to 13, joining a lute and the koel, are hard to construe.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man leaves home to labour across the waste

comparisons.tenor: her soft walk, like a fine female swan's
the burning resolve in his heart, which the rain of effort did not put out

occasion.words: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

280.reading: Having seen the girl with her garland of gold-bright serunthi playing at chasing crabs on the shore, the man tells his heart that since even a shipload of wealth would not win her, he will leave his country, plough salt and go into the deep sea on a float with her father, and serve him humbly, in the hope that the fisherman who shares out pearls on the wide shore will give her to him.
280.nuance: A suitor proposes to earn a bride by servitude, not by bride-price, because the father's pride makes wealth useless; அறம் தெரிந்து makes the humbling a matter of right conduct, not of desperation.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குந் தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது. அல்லகுறிப்பட்டுப் போகாநின்றவன் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: crabs, salt pans and the fisherman of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the serunthi blossoms of her garland, like beaten gold

occasion.words: தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குந் தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

links.note: Both are Paranar's and both use Anni Minili, whose father the Kosar blinded and whose vow Thithiyan fulfilled: in 196 the wife names the courtesan as one who carries herself like Minili; in 262 the lover's joy is like Minili's when her anger was released.
links.teaches: One poet draws on either half of the same local revenge story, the proud wrath in 196 and the relief after vengeance in 262, so the story was known well enough to be cited by a single name for a single mood.

links.note: Purananuru 142 (Paranar) praises Pekan as giving like rain that falls everywhere without choosing; Akananuru 262 (Paranar) gives Pekan's hill as கொண்டல் மாமலை, the rain-cloud hill whose drizzle wets the bushes, and lends its scent to the girl's voice.
links.teaches: The same poet's figure for Pekan's indiscriminate giving, rain, is carried into akam as the smell of his rain-soaked hill, showing a patron's praise-image reused as a lover's sensory measure.

links.note: Purananuru 233 is a lament that wishes false the dawn report of Evvi's many wounds; Akananuru 266 measures the gossip about the husband by the roar of the feast at Uraththur after Evvi's victory.
links.teaches: Evvi's name travels with loud public report in both books, a victory feast in akam and a death rumour in puram, so the akam poet uses his fame precisely as a gauge of how far news spreads.

links.note: Purananuru 264 sets up a stone for a man who recovered cattle, crowned with red flowers tied with marral fibre and peacock feather and inscribed with his name; Akananuru 269 shows such stones on the road, names inscribed, washed, smeared with turmeric and crowned with red karanthai for men who held off the Mazhavar to recover cattle.
links.teaches: The puram poem gives the stone on the day of grief, when the bards still come not knowing; the akam poem shows the same rite kept up later on a travelled road, so together they show the hero-stone moving from mourning to a standing roadside cult.

links.note: Akananuru 270 names Kazhumalam as the town of Kuttuvan, the Chera, as a figure of beauty; Akananuru 44 tells how the Chola Senni took Kazhumalam after capturing Kanaiyan, and uses Senni's Azhumbil as its simile.
links.teaches: The same town appears as a Chera possession in one akam simile and as a Chola conquest in another, so the similes preserve a contested place under rival owners and are evidence for its history, not only ornament.

links.note: Purananuru 343, a maganmaruttal poem, has the father refuse his daughter even if suitors bow and give நலஞ்சால் விழுப்பொருள்; Akananuru 280 has the lover say she cannot be had even for நலம்சால் விழுப்பொருள் given by the shipload, and resolve to serve her fisherman father instead.
links.teaches: The near-identical phrase shows the akam suitor speaking inside the puram convention of the father who refuses wealth, and gives the convention's other side: where puram suitors bring siege, the akam lover answers the refusal with servitude.

links.note: Kural 1007 likens the wealth of a man who gives nothing to the needy to a beautiful woman growing old alone; the courtesan in Akananuru 276 likens her own beauty, if she fails to win the man, to the wealth of one who hoarded and never gave to those who asked.
links.teaches: The two verses run the same comparison in opposite directions, beauty as vehicle for hoarded wealth in the Kural and hoarded wealth as vehicle for beauty in the poem, which shows the pairing was a shared idea in which each term could explain the other.

links.note: Kural 1147 has the woman say her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water; in Akananuru 273 she says the sickness sprouted between her breasts, grew a trunk, spread branches of gossip and budded with scandal into a tree shading the world.
links.teaches: The Kural's two-line plant metaphor, gossip feeding the disease, is the seed of Avvaiyar's full tree, which adds the stages of growth and makes the scandal not only food for the love but its flowering.

links.note: In Kural 1236 the woman tells her friend that with bangles and shoulders slackening what hurts is hearing him called cruel; in Akananuru 267, when the friend says the oath-breaker has changed, the wife replies that he is not at fault and her shoulders, which let the bangles slip, are.
links.teaches: Same speaker, addressee and occasion: the Kural states the defence of the absent man as a feeling, and the poem shows its rhetorical move, turning the blame on her own body, so the couplet's restraint is seen as an argument with the friend.

links.note: Kural 1151 (the friend's words for Parimelazhagar) tells the departing man to promise his quick return to those who will still be alive; in Akananuru 271, the friend tells the departing man to prosper, but asks whether there is any medicine for the girl in the land where he will stay.
links.teaches: Both turn the farewell into a threat of her death, but the poem argues it through the road, whose nelli fruit revives dying travellers, so the couplet's bare warning is given a reason: the waste has remedies for strangers and none for her.

links.note: Both are a mother after her daughter's elopement: in 263 she says she would gladly have married the girl to the youth had she known; in 275 she recalls the girl's play and lisping speech and points onlookers to the sand house the girl left.
links.teaches: Read together they give the mother's two answers to the loss, regret that she was not asked and grief over the childhood left behind, so the elopement is a wound to her authority as well as to her love.

links.note: In 261 the man, back home, recalls the girl on the elopement road too shy to walk ahead of him, while a tiger roared and bowmen's drums sounded; in 275 the mother imagines her daughter on the bear-haunted hot road and is left with her sand house.
links.teaches: The same journey is seen from both ends: for the mother the road is only danger and loss, while the man remembers it as the girl's shyness and a slow camp in the wild, so the anthology lets each speaker hold the half the other cannot know.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage as the end of secret love; the friend's pressing of the lover to marry (வரைவு கடாயது)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons' word (வரைவு கடாயது); the verses imply it

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place of secret lovers, by day (பகற்குறி) or by night (இரவுக்குறி)
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons' word; the verses name day and night meetings

new_concepts.gloss: the hero-stone raised where a warrior fell, inscribed with his name, washed, anointed and garlanded
new_concepts.label_source: Akananuru 269 line 7 (நெடுங்கல், the stone that looks planted, நட்ட போலும்); the usual name is நடுகல்

source_issues: 266: the colophon thurai says தலைமகன் சொல்லியது, but the speaker addresses the husband (மகிழ்ந, line 9) and complains of his oath; it should read தலைமகள் சொல்லியது. thurai_akam gives thalaivi.
271: the colophon thurai begins with a stray alternative number (1செலவுணர்த்திய) and gives no second alternative.
275: the colophon thurai has a stray numeral (1தாய்) and gives no second alternative.
276: the colophon thurai reads தலைமகட்ருப், a misprint for தலைமகட்குப்.
272: line 18 spells மஞ்ஜை with ஜ for the usual மஞ்ஞை.
275: lines 4 and 5 (இளமைத் தகைமையை வளமனைக் கிழத்தி; பிதிர்வை நீரை வெண்நீறு ஆக) are obscure, perhaps corrupt; who is addressed is unclear.
